nameStory: The name 'daisy' comes from the Old English 'daes eage,' meaning 'day's eye,' because these cheerful flowers open with the sunrise and close at dusk. 'Lawn daisy' simply describes where we most often encounter them - scattered across our grasses like tiny white stars. The scientific name Bellis perennis means 'pretty and lasting,' which perfectly captures this persistent little bloomer.
description: Lawn daisy is a low-growing perennial wildflower that forms small rosettes close to the ground. Each plant produces classic white daisy flowers with bright yellow centers on short stems, typically reaching only 2-6 inches tall. Originally from Europe, this hardy little plant has made itself completely at home in New England lawns, parks, and grassy areas. The flowers are small but numerous, creating a charming carpet effect when many plants grow together.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Classic daisy shape with 15-30 narrow white petals (technically ray petals) surrounding a raised yellow center. Flowers are about 3/4 inch across and feel slightly papery when touched, closing up at night and in cloudy weather.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small spoon-shaped leaves arranged in a tight rosette at ground level. Leaves feel slightly fuzzy and have shallow scalloped edges, growing directly from the base with no stem leaves.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, flat rosettes that hug the ground, rarely exceeding 6 inches tall. Multiple flower stems arise from each rosette, creating clusters of blooms that feel springy underfoot.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny seeds without the fluffy parachutes of dandelions. Seeds are smooth and oval-shaped, dispersed when the spent flower heads are disturbed by wind or foot traffic.

habitat: Thrives in short grass areas like lawns, parks, playing fields, and meadow edges throughout New England. Prefers moist, fertile soils but tolerates a wide range of conditions from full sun to partial shade. Often found mixed with other low-growing plants like clover and plantain in disturbed or regularly mowed areas.

seasonality.spring: Begins blooming in early spring as soon as the weather warms, often appearing in March and April. Fresh green rosettes emerge and flower buds start opening with the longer days.
seasonality.summer: Continues blooming steadily through summer, though may slow down during hot, dry periods. Flowers open and close daily, creating a reliable show of white and yellow.
seasonality.fall: Keeps producing flowers well into fall, often blooming until the first hard frost. Seeds ripen and disperse throughout the season, preparing for next year's plants.
seasonality.winter: Rosettes often remain green under snow cover, going dormant but staying alive. In milder winters, may even produce occasional flowers during warm spells.

funFact: Lawn daisies can actually predict the weather - the flowers close tightly when rain is approaching, sometimes hours before the first drops fall, because the petals are sensitive to changes in humidity and air pressure!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with fleabane daisies, but lawn daisies are much smaller, grow in tight ground-hugging rosettes, and have broader white petals. Remember: lawn daisies stay low and close to the ground, while fleabanes grow tall with leafy stems.
contextualKnowledge: Though often considered a lawn 'weed' by some homeowners, lawn daisies are actually beneficial plants that provide early nectar for bees and other pollinators when few other flowers are available. In many cultures, they're symbols of innocence and are the classic flower used for 'loves me, loves me not' games.
compareHints: Lawn daisy is the only Bellis species commonly found in New England. Compared to other small white daisies in the Asteraceae family, it's distinguished by its ground-hugging rosette growth pattern and relatively few, broad white petals. Unlike asters or fleabanes, lawn daisies never develop tall, branching stems and always keep their leaves clustered at the base.
